utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody around the court. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances for this morning, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Laurie Sartorio and Matthias Neuner for the Prosecution, with our case manager, Alma Imamovic. And we are assisted by our intern, Anna Svensson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to our colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor and to all in the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for the Defence of General Delic, assisted by Ms. Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, may we remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony, to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just two topics remain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Duncan, yesterday I put to you that you didn't know for certain whether the Mujahedin or, indeed, the 7th Muslim Brigade existed, and you replied: "No. It's on the record. This is eight years ago for me, and if that's what I said, that's what I said." Do you recall giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If the witness could please be shown Exhibit 293, please. This is the milinfosum dated 27th of June, 1993. Your Honours, it's not displayed on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Neither is it on the screen of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not the document that I was looking for. It was the milinfosum dated the 27th of June, 1993, number 59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it already an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It is. It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You called for Exhibit 293.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise if I am referring to the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has a hard copy of the document from the 27th of June, 1993, if this would assist my learned colleague. You can place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, Exhibit 293, Mr. Robson, was an Annex A to milinfosum number 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want the ORBAT order?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 290, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 290.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So first of all we can just confirm that this is the document that I'm talking about, and please if we could proceed to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, that's not it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document we see on the screen is the one that I wish to refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Duncan, on this page what we can see is the Order of Battle for the 7th Muslim Brigade as assessed by one of your officers; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we discussed this during your evidence yesterday, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and we pointed out the nomenclature of all those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, having told us that you were not aware or are not aware whether or not the 7th Muslim Brigade existed, is it right to say that you cannot confirm that the commander of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade in Travnik was Asim Korcic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I cannot confirm that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if I suggest to you that Asim Korcic was not even in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time this report was prepared, can you refute that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't refute that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've finished with this document. Perhaps it could be put away, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I turn to the final topic, and that concerns Guca Gora. Mr. Duncan, in your evidence yesterday you told us about a number of Croats sheltering in a church at Guca Gora --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- in June 1993, and what you said was, I quote: "My call signs, which were there on the ground, detected that there was going to be a problem here because these people could well be massacred." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown Exhibit 292, please. Your Honours, if we can just quickly look at the first page of this document, we can see if -- this is Annex A to the milinfosum dated the 8th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you remember this document from yesterday, Mr. Duncan?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can turn to the second page of this document, please. Now, the entry that I'm interested in is the one in the middle of the screen, and that we can see that the six-figure number there is "081601." If I could just read out this extract, it says: "A CS attempting to reach Guca Gora is held up by Muslims in the village of Mosor, who formed a human wall. Women lay in front of the Warriors to prevent them leaving the area as they fear a potential massacre by Croats." Now, Mr. Duncan, yesterday you told us about Guca Gora, but it's right to say that Muslim villages in that area were also under attack, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can look at the extract a little further down the screen, the six-figure number is "081905," we can see though it says: "CO 1 PWO takes the decision to deploy Warrior overnight in Guca Gora and Mosor to prevent any chance of a massacre." So it's correct, Mr. Duncan, that you took the decision to leave your vehicles in both Guca Gora and Mosor, the Muslim village, as well?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If this document could be put away. I'd like to refer to another one, please. This is a Prosecution document. It wasn't entered into evidence. It's P1180. Your Honours, this is a document from the assistant commander for security to the brigade commanders of -- and one of the operative groups. It's a document that's in both English and B/C/S. Perhaps the B/C/S version could also be put on the screen as well, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Apparently there's some technical problem with the B/C/S, and assistance is being sought to sort that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Duncan, would you agree that this document is dated the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that from the top left-hand box, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, unfortunately on this English document, if we scroll to the bottom of the page, the person who prepared this document is not named, but I believe if we were to look at the B/C/S version, we would be able to ascertain who the document is from. I understand it's not possible to scroll down. Your Honour, what I would like to put to this witness is that this document was prepared by somebody called "Salko Bebe."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it not possible to scroll down the B/C/S, to the bottom of that? There's a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can focus on the bottom part, Mr. Duncan, it is difficult to see, but would you agree that that document appears to be -- appears to come from somebody called "Bebe, Salko"?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is he somebody that you know?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: He's somebody that you had dealings with?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, please, if we could return back to the English version, if we can only get that one on the screen, and it's the top half of the document. Now, we can see there a number of dashes, and it's the third dash down that I'm interested in. In this document what Mr. Bebe says is that: "Units of the 306th Mountain Brigade have captured Gornja Gora and continue to advance towards Nova Bila. Measures are being taken to prevent looting and the mistreatment of Croats who have remained in the town; persons who demolished the church have been arrested." So, Mr. Duncan, would you agree with me when I say that according to this officer, when he wrote this report on the 8th of June, he indicated that steps were being taken to prevent mistreatment of Croats in that place?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, could this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 304.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Duncan, during your time as commander of Brit-Bat, is it right that you worked closely with the ECMM in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We had a detachment with us in the Vitez school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And were you familiar with the coordination centre in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly, but I was aware there was something there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Were you aware that the head of the coordination centre in Travnik was a former British officer by the name of Philip Watkins?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is -- I do remember that name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is he somebody you met whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet him while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right to say, isn't it, that the ECMM had a specific mandate to monitor reports of atrocities being committed in the Central Bosnia area; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage if we could please go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: This is my final document today. If Exhibit 293 could be brought up, please. This is a -- by way of explanation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, I'm just looking at the witness's last reply to your question as to whether Croat civilians could well have been massacred in Guca Gora, and the witness, General Duncan, answered, "Yes," to your question of whether Croat civilians could well have been massacred in Guca Gora. I'm not exactly sure how to interpret the meaning of your question and certainly the answer of it by the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document contradicts that allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't see how the document the you have shown could contradict the suggestion that the civilians could have. I guess they could. But for one reason or another, they weren't. But, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm glad -- I'm grateful for the opportunity to clarify this. Perhaps we should return back to the document. It would mean having to go back into private session, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: As I say, the document I'd like to refer to is Exhibit 293, and this is Annex A to milinfosum 41 dated 9 June 1993. It's the first entry that I'm interested in. It states "Sitrep."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's "Situation report," is it not it, Mr. Duncan?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: "The situation has remained calm overnight in the Bila valley. There are still approximately 150 Croats in the church of Guca Gora, some of whom are HVO soldiers who have changed into civilian clothing and have handed over their weapons. The BiH are allowing some Croats to return to their houses to collect possessions and food." Now, would you agree with me, General Duncan, that in a situation where you have the Bosnian Army allowing Croat civilians to return to their houses to collect possessions and food, this doesn't sound as though it's a case that the Bosnian Army was wishing to massacre those civilians, does it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what is said there, no, but I would remind you that I've already said that we were being fired at during the day, the church and my people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It rather indicates that the Bosnian Army was taking care and protection over those Bosnian Croats, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that, in turn, I would say begs the question as why those people in that church were afraid of their future. They were scared and frightened, which is why they were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. Any re-examination, Mr. Neuner?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning. First of all, Witness, I wish to excuse Mr. Mundis, who left yesterday afternoon, and asked me to do the re-examination today. My name is Matthias Neuner, and I'm going to put a couple of questions to you. You were asked yesterday by my learned colleague about the history of the conflict in early 1993, the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH. You replied, and this is on page 60, line 12-13: "The only conflict I knew which had gone on was Ahmici." I wish to show you document PT1082. While it is coming up, I can introduce the document briefly. It's a document dating 27th of April from Brit-Bat, and we can see here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which year, Mr. Neuner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And we can see here that it is being sent to Brit-For Split on the first page, and to the headquarters in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And if we could please scroll down on the first page in the English version, and I'm interested in the 10th line from the bottom. It starts with: "Brit-Bat personnel under the direction of UNHCR ...," and I read it to you: "Brit-Bat personnel, under the direction of UNHCR, moved 23 Bosniak Croat civilians from Miletici to Nova Bila. The five Bosnian Croat corpses which resulted from the attack on Miletici were moved to the local cemetery by Brit-Bat."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to object to this particular question. My line of questioning yesterday related to combat activities in the Bila Valley, which the witness stated was the western part of the Lasva Valley, in early June 1993. Miletici was not mentioned, and I don't accept that that was a military action, so hence I don't see how this question arises out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say Miletici was not a military action?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: My response would be that you had asked this witness whether he can recall any early combat action between the HVO and the ABiH, and you were referring -- or you got an answer relating to Ahmici, and I'm referring just here to a document from Brit-Bat, from that exact time period, it's the time period of Ahmici, and I'm trying to explore whether this witness recalls the incident. And as I can see here, also, and this would be a question I would have as well, the five Bosnian Croat corpses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: -- resulted in an attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Neuner, we're dealing with an objection right now. Don't carry on with the examination, yet. What's your position? Is it your position that Miletici was a military action or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This document alleges this, and I was trying to explore this with this witness. It's not necessarily the Prosecution's position, but since this is a Brit-Bat document, authored at the time this witness was in his position, I thought the witness could shed some light on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Do you have any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could respond briefly. First of all, it was the Prosecution that raised the issue of Ahmici, not the Defence, Your Honours. Also, looking at this document, it doesn't appear to me to suggest that Brit-Bat considered this to be an action between the HVO and the BiH. So I fail to see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I haven't read this document, but I think I'm going to allow the question. The objection is overruled. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: First of all, my first question is: Have you seen that document?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- I'm sure I would have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. And can you confirm it's a Brit-Bat document?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a Brit-Bat document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The information provided here on the first page, who at the time would have compiled that information?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll up slightly, that might... It would be put together by the intelligence cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It says here: "Drafter, Ruddock." Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have been one of the staff in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning back to the incident of Miletici I've just read out, do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't particularly recall it, because in terms of what was going on at that time, it was a relatively minor incident within the -- what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It says that five corpses were moved to a local cemetery by Brit-Bat. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That action of moving bodies for both sides, as it were, to make sure that they got back to their own people, was something we did quite a lot of in those early days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And it says 23 Croats are moved from Miletici to Nova Bila. Can you explain what that might mean?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might well mean that they were again probably in fear of their -- of being attacked, and that's their perception, and we would have moved them out of harm's way that might come.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And Nova Bila at this point in time, late April 1993, who held Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nova Bila was -- I can't tell you, it depends which exact date it was, but it shifted left and right, as it were, between the factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So if it states that Croats are moved to that location by Brit-Bat here in the document, 23 Croats are moved from Miletici to Nova Bila, who at this point in time would hold Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: As the witness just answered, "I don't know." I object to this line of questioning because Mr. Duncan has very clearly said that he doesn't recall this incident, so the Prosecutor is inviting him to speculate on what may or may not have happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm not pursuing this line of questioning, but I would ask that this document please be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think I must uphold the objection. I think you were inviting speculation. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 306.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were shown Exhibit 302, a document from the 28th of May, 1993, and at page 110 of yesterday's transcript you were asked about General Alagic and whether the system of command and control was breaking down in Travnik at the end of May 1993. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. I wish to show you another exhibit, Exhibit 294. While this is being shown, pulled up, I can inform you this is again a milinfosum, number 39, and dates from the 7th of June, so roughly a week after the document Exhibit 302 which had been shown to you yesterday. And I'm interested in paragraph 3, first of all, on the first page. On the 7th of June, it is reported here: "In general the situation is calmer with the town of Travnik reportedly free of fighting and civilian movement ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In general, do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 4, it is stated that an HVO headquarter from Commander Leutar in Jankovici had been completely demolished. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 4(a), it states: "That the BiH now exclusively controls the town of Travnik ..." Do you recall this as well?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So my question to you is: What made the BiH Army control Travnik on the 7th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the BiH had effective control, military control, of the town of Travnik at that stage, and therefore that -- and the Croats had been expelled from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And where was the headquarter of General Alagic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an old JNA barracks. I don't exactly know the name, but I often visited that headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In what town was it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I wish to go back to the document Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a document that was introduced by the -- into evidence by the Defence, and I wish to correct the record, lest the Tribunal be misled. This was the document that we discussed in connection with Croat and Serb cooperation and Croat civilians crossing the Serb lines. The question that my learned friend put to Mr. Duncan seems to suggest that the HVO HQ was demolished as a result of ABiH action, and Mr. Duncan told us that Croats were expelled. If we can look at point B of the document, the comment there is: "The HVO blew up their own HQ in order to stop anything of value falling into BiH hands." I think this matter needs to be explored before a misunderstanding of the situation arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Duncan, you have just heard this paragraph B which was partially read out to you. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I mean, destroying your headquarters and moving out is quite a normal thing to do. You would not leave behind anything of value for the enemy to use, and therefore any communications that you couldn't get out or other equipment that you couldn't use would be destroyed, and you would then move away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: My learned friend just asked this in relation to your use of the word "expelled."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Would you still hold the position that --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would, that they were expelled, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move to another document now which was just shown, Exhibit 305.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This is under seal, Your Honours, so it may be worth to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: While Exhibit 301 is being displayed, I can inform you a document you have seen, I believe yesterday, from the 19th of May, 1993, from Brit-Bat, and I have just a question relating to paragraph 2, which is called "Joint Commission for Bosnia-Herzegovina." You have several times referred to the joint commission. Could you say what the mandate of the Joint Commission for Bosnia-Herzegovina was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry. If you could spare me one moment, please. Your Honour, if I'm wrong, I'll stand corrected, but my recollection is that I did not raise the issue of the Joint Commission at all, so again this appears to be another situation where my learned friend appears to be using one document that we referred to as a springboard to launch off into another area that was not dealt with during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, is the Joint Commission referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It is referred to in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, deal with it in the same way as we dealt with the previous, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you briefly transcribe the mandate of the Joint Commission as mentioned in this report?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Joint Commission was a commission, I believe, between the BiH and the HVO. Apart from them trying to work together, to work together, I do not know what the mandate of the commission is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you meet members of this commission?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recognise some of the names on both sides here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Which names do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halilovic, Totic, and that is it at the moment. I can't recall any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And who was Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was a BiH commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, I haven't really understood why there were these refugees in the Guca Gora church. Had they been expelled from their houses?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they had been expelled from their houses, and they had gathered together as a bunch into the church, where they felt they would be protected. The reason they felt they would be protected in the church is that my -- Brit-Bat were surrounding the church and therefore making it a safe area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but to your knowledge who expelled them? Do you know who expelled them from their houses?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically who expelled them at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. General, your testimony during these two days have been very interesting, but they have left some traces of doubt in my mind, and this is why I would like to put some last questions to you, to clarify the uncertainty. You are well aware of the fact that the accused in this case is charged, among other things, exactly with failure to control the activities of some of the alleged crimes committed by the Mujahedin. And this is why your testimony about the degree of control is of particular importance. You started out, as I recall, by asserting that, in your view, at least the 3rd Corps and possibly also at higher echelons of authority, the ABiH was very much in control of the activities of the Mujahedin. I think these were your words, "very much in control." During cross-examination, however, counsel for the Defence presented you with a series of documents, and your comments to these documents, as I recall, would leave some doubt as to just how much in control was the 3rd Corps or the ABiH, as such, really in control of the Mujahedin, and this is why in order -- before you leave us, I would like to try these questions on you again and say do you -- and ask you: Do you maintain the very firm position that you started out with, that you still think that the 3rd Corps was very much in control of the Mujahedin, or the ABiH, at some higher level, was very much in control of the ABiH [sic]?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, thank you. I'm very much aware of some of the comments that have been taken from my previous paper and previous attendance in this Chamber, when I have obviously stated what I believed it was then. It is in the space of some 15 years since I was actually in Bosnia. It's -- the memory obviously fades, but there are some things that I still feel, and some areas where I feel, that the Muslim Brigade, as it was, was used as a very effective weapon by the ABiH during that conflict. Whether it was used physically or just as a threat or to move around to frighten people, I don't know, but I think it was used in such a manner. And I would expect that to be done in a manner which enables the best activity from that corps. Because it is of such value as a fighting unit and as a propaganda unit, I still believe it would have been held at a very high level in order to be able to complete its activities as best as possible. Therefore, it would be used with care on high-value targets, et cetera, et cetera. I still believe that that's how it was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Two questions arise out of your answer. The first question is: Who are you referring to when you say "the Muslim Brigade"? There was something called the 7th Muslim Brigade and then there was the Mujahedin Detachment. Which of the two are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the 7th Muslim Brigade. As to the -- whether there were Mujahid, I've stated on record that I've never actually seen a Mujahid, and that is very difficult. It's very difficult to say that person is a Mujahid or that person isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My second question, then, relates to what you make yourself of the evidence shown to you that the Mujahedin actually were uncontrollable and apparently acted very independently?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, a certain amount of evidence has -- has indicated that way, but not, to my mind, in a firm manner, if that makes sense, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you clarify a bit?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you reset the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. I understand you to say -- this is my interpretation of your answer. I understand you to say that at least some of the activities of the Mujahedin must have been coordinated at some level because of the effect of having a force that was known to be quite violent.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So I understand you to say, to this part of your testimony, is that if you actually dispose over such a frightful force, then that can be used very efficiently, and the way it was used on the ground seems to suggest that there must have been some sort of coordination. That is how I hear you.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question to you was, then: Well, how does this correspond with the evidence that we have seen during your testimony, that at least at some other actions, the Mujahedin acted just as they wanted to, independently and clearly without the ability of the ABiH to control them. So how is that reconcilable?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very -- it is very difficult for us, my soldiers on the ground, when they come across an incident, to know whether that incident has been perpetrated by A, B, or C. I don't know. They would merely report back what they had seen and what had happened, and therefore we couldn't always put a tag straightaway on something, "That's clearly Mujahid," or, "That's clearly HVO," or, "That's clearly ABiH would have done that attack or that incident," and it is difficult, therefore, to put a firm tab on those things and say that's actually what happened. In many cases people were reporting back what they saw, and we would try and put things together. It was, for all of us, a very confusing period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That I accept. But it wasn't just a question -- it wasn't just a matter of investigating who was responsible exactly for which action. The evidence that was brought to you yesterday and today would suggest that it wasn't only the Brit-Bat or your own people who had this perception of the Mujahedin of being inaccessible, it was all the way around; UNHCR, UNPROFOR, everybody who tried to deal with the Mujahedin were all told that they would not be given a very warm welcome.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I agree that that perception was agreed by everybody during that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So here we have it. There is a perception that is widely accepted, that they were inaccessible and uncontrollable, yet you say that there must have been some sort of coordination to guide their actions?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And this is the crux of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And I would like you to explore a bit on it.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are -- there are, and you've just explained it, a body of belief across the area we are looking at which people believed that the Muslims and the Mujahid were out of control. We always tried, as a unit, to make sure we reported back exactly what we saw, as I've just said. Over those months that I was there, the seven months or so, I still believed that this corps, this very effective organisation, was being used at a high level, because it is like a special forces, they are very, very carefully used over selective targets and used in that manner. And I really -- I can't -- so, I'm sorry, I can't explain it any better than that and it's probably not very helpful, which is unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think this is about a convenient time to take a break. We'll come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: --- Resumed at 10.46 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Lattanzi, you still have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please excuse me, but I still have a question I'd like to put to you. I'm still a bit confused about some matters after listening to your latest answers, and I'm thinking in particular of the 7th Muslim Brigade and of the Mujahedin. There is still some confusion remaining, it seems to me, in terms of these two units. And the first question I wanted to put to you was as follows: You mentioned investigations conducted on the ground. You said it was difficult to find out who had done what. But when it comes to the facts that are at the heart of this case, in order to determine whether the Mujahedin were responsible, you were not in a position to say that they were responsible or if they were responsible, because you were not aware that they were in Bosnia, you were not aware of their presence in Bosnia; is that what you said? In other words, my question -- sorry, I'll rephrase my question in a more clearer manner. My question is whether those who committed or seemed to have committed these crimes, whether Mujahedin or not, you were not able to determine whether that was the case in your unit, you were not in a position to answer that question, because you stated here -- you repeated here what you stated in a previous case in this Tribunal. You repeated that you were not aware that the Mujahedin were present on the ground because you were not in a position to make a distinction between those who were members of the Mujahedin and the others, you were not in a position to make a distinction between the various factions?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, because I was very seldom able to get to any of those locations where incidents might have happened. I had to rely upon my troops, when they were on the ground, reporting back, and they recorded what they had seen and we put that into the milinfosums, which is why the milinfosum is so important, reporting, to get a body of evidence of perhaps of what's going on. But you're entirely right to say that I personally can't say, with my hand on my heart, that I ever saw a Mujahedin, because I hadn't. I was never in a position to see one, as it were, because my job was not to go out personally on the ground, it was to control events and try and stop things happening that shouldn't happen, to prevent more fighting, to make sure the aid got through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you're saying about your own personal position, but talking about your battalion, did you receive reports about the presence and the participation in the fighting of foreign individuals that were named "Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive -- get reports from my soldiers on the ground of such people fighting, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One further question. Judge Harhoff asked you a question, and when answering that last question of his, you referred to the Mujahedin. And here I'm slightly confused, because I had believed that you were referring to the 7th Muslim Brigade at first, but here apparently you are referring to the Mujahedin. I apologise, but this is really a question of vital importance for this case, and we need things to be clarified. We need to be able to make a difference, the distinction between the 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin. Judge Harhoff put a question to you, and you stated, in answering that question -- you stated the following. Well, his question was about the fact that they were inaccessible and uncontrollable. Referring to this "they" mentioned here, later on you said, "I believe that the Muslims and the Mujahedin were out of control" -- no, sorry, no, sorry, that was the question put to you by Judge Harhoff. When listening to you, I got the impression that the Muslims and the Mujahedin were out of control. That's what Judge Harhoff said to you. And then you keep talking about the Muslims and the Mujahedin, and I'd like to understand. I do not understand. Are you talking about the Mujahedin or are you talking about the 7th Muslim Corps? That's what I'd really would like to know.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was a corps -- the 7th Muslim Brigade was a fighting unit of the ABiH that was composed of BiH soldiers. Within that brigade, and most of them were Muslims, there were perhaps 10 per cent, I believe - I can't verify it - something like 10 per cent who were Mujahid and would represent in clothing and behaviour. So you would have the 7th Muslim Brigade with an element of outsiders who have come in and may be polluting that brigade and causing incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Therefore, you are talking about individuals who you call "Mujahids" and were members of the 7th Muslim Brigade; you're not talking about the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking of the 7th Muslim Brigade, Madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to have to pursue that question a little more, because that's what I also wanted to get clarity on. And there's a springboard to that question. Let me refer you to the question by Judge Harhoff, where he says and this is at page 32, starting at line 9. He says: "Two questions arise out of your answer. The first question is: Who are you referring to when you say 'the Muslim Brigade'? There was something called the 7th Muslim Brigade, and then there was the Mujahedin Detachment. Which of the two are we talking about?" Your answer was: "I'm referring to the 7th Muslim Brigade. As to whether there were Mujahid, I have stated on record that I have never actually seen a Mujahid, and that is very difficult -- it's very difficult to say that that person is a Mujahid or that person isn't." Now, I just want to put something very clearly to you here. Within Bosnia at the time, the allegations are that there was what was called "The 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade" which was a part of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you have said that according to your knowledge, that brigade had some 10 per cent outside Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I believe, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what you believe. Then apart from that, and I'm not asking you about whether you know of -- you have seen a Mujahid person, I'm asking you now about a unit, there was also within Bosnia what was called "The El Mujahedin Detachment" --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- which was a detachment, and this is the subject of this case. Now, my question to you is: Were you aware of the existence of a unit called "The El Mujahedin Detachment"?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I was not aware of that designation, but I was aware of reports and sightings of a number of so-called Mujahid groups, I mean small groups, around the place, which came back from my soldiers. They would mention, for example, sir, that, "We had been at a check-point and there were a group of Mujahid in the background," and it would be four or five people, these sort of sightings, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, we have heard evidence --.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- of various groups of --.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- for lack of a better word, what were called Arab units --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But they were not exclusively Arab. They came from various countries. But of interest to us is what is called -- they called it "The EMD," "The El Mujahedin Detachment." Now, you say, as you sit there, you are not aware and were not aware at the time of the existence of this unit that is called "The El Mujahedin Detachment"?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when you talk of Mujahedin in your evidence right through your testimony, you were actually referring to the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So wherever we see the word "Mujahid" or "Mujahedin" used by you, we can safely substitute "7th Muslim Brigade" for that word?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from those who were in those small groups that I've just discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. What is your basis for assuming that the Mujahedin persons belonged to the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the numbers, sir, that were seen when my liaison officers were around and able to see that brigade. There were numbers of -- within that estimated 10 per cent or so that were the Mujahedin in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How am I to understand this? Do you mean to say that your people, when they were patrolling the territory or the area, they saw Mujahedin persons, Arabs, as we have come to call them in this trial?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: They saw Arabs, and when they saw Arabs, there were always people from the 7th Muslim Brigade also present at this point; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were normally part of the 7th Muslim Brigade, but I would refer back to these occasional groups, five or six, that might be dotted about in other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. But, you see, my wish is to understand how you link these groups or Arab individuals with the 7th Muslim Brigade. That's what I want to be sure that I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe, sir, that -- that roughly 10 per cent within the 7th Muslim Brigade were Mujahedin, in terms of being much more fanatical than others within that brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But how do you know they were the 7th Muslim.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were part of it and seen along side others within that brigade, and the commanders there would -- we would talk. My liaison officers would talk with the commanders and discuss, "Oh, yes, where has he been," and, "Where has he come from," and things like that. It was just discussions almost every day across the entire organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The heart of the matter is whether, in your view and having your knowledge, these individual or groups of Arabs could have acted outside as not being members of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- that is possible if they would be detached for an operation at a higher level than within 3rd Corps. They could well have been picked up and moved to do a different task. Therefore, they have taken outside of 3rd Corps and given another task from something above or somewhere above. That is quite feasible. As an officer commanding, that is quite normal, to take somebody for a specific task, move them out, get that task fulfilled, and then put them back where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you aware of any evidence to show this?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that that's what happened, because you would find that the bits of the Muslim Brigade we thought were going to be there weren't and had moved away, and we would have to track them down and see where they'd got to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One small point. You're talking about the Mujahedin who were part of the 7th Muslim Brigade. Are you talking about local Mujahedin or are you referring to Arabs, because I've never heard you use the word "Arab."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never used the word "Arab" at all. You're quite right, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The other part of the question was: Are you referring to local Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult to -- it was relatively easy, rather, to see and identify those people who were dressed in Arab clothes within the Muslim Brigade. At the same time, there would be others outside of that brigade, on blocks and things, who may well not have been Muslims at all but were dressed, because it was the thing to do, in the Muslim manner, because they thought it was tough and macho and all the rest of it, and that was -- and so that was local boys in many cases, young people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions arising from the questions by the Bench, Mr. Neuner?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have a question to the Bench first. Is it allowed to use a document which was not on the exhibit list as submitted by my -- I see Mr. Harhoff says, "No." Then the Prosecution has no further questions. We would have, relating to that topic, a document, which we could show to this witness, which touches upon the issue of coordination, Supreme Command, 3rd Corps, but we are aware that this is not on Mr. Mundis' exhibit list, and so therefore I would have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just two matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: There's a high degree of confusion about your evidence, Mr. Duncan, but from what you've told us, you did not personally see a foreign Mujahedin fighter. You also told us earlier that you didn't know whether or not the Mujahedin existed. It's right to say, isn't it, when you said that the command of the Mujahedin was at a higher level, that amounts to pure speculation, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that as a military commander, part of my being here is to be able to give evidence on that part of being a military commander, and it is my opinion that a brigade like that would be used like that. But it's an opinion, it's a comment, and we've talked about comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, you're not here as an expert witness, are you? And you would agree with me that what was happening in Central Bosnia and Bosnia as a whole was not a normal situation in the way that would understand a NATO-styled military conflict to be run; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then the last matter, just in response to a question from one of the Judges, you said that, "That's why the milinfosum is so important, reporting, to get a body of evidence of perhaps what's going on." The fact is, Mr. Duncan, that the creation of the milinfosum was not to create evidence, was it, or gather evidence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was, it was to gather -- sorry, it wasn't to gather evidence. It was to gather facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And as you explained in your evidence yesterday, the purpose for gathering facts was to enable Brit-Bat to create the conditions for aid to be delivered?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you just bear with me one moment. Those are my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This brings us to the conclusion of your testimony, Mr. Duncan. Thank you very much for taking time off your very busy schedule to come and testify, and you are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. We have our witnesses who should be ready --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We need the next witness to be brought in, Mr. Djuricic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Zdravko Djuricic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And where were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you please briefly tell the Chamber about your education and your post -- education post that you held in your field of study?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school, secondary school, and law school in Sarajevo. After that I worked as a trainee in a court of law. And then I was a judge for about four years, I think. After that, I worked in the Ministry of Justice. At that time, it was called "The Secretariat for the Judiciary." I worked there for five years. I worked on the supervision of regular courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina. After that, I went to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where I worked as secretary of the Commission for Pardons. Then -- at the same time, rather, I was adviser for general legal affairs in the Presidency. When the war started, I became deputy secretary general of the Presidency and after that the secretary general of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can we just get some dates in here in terms of when you finished law school and when you worked at the Ministry of Justice and then when you started working at the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I got my law degree in 1974, I think it was. Then I did my military service. When I returned from the army, I took my first job as a trainee. I think that was in 1976. In 1977, I was already a judge. In 1981 I worked in the Ministry of Justice, and then in 1985, I think, in the Presidency. And then in 1992, I became deputy secretary general, and I think it was also in 1992 that I became secretary general of the Presidency, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how long were you the deputy and secretary general, in terms of the year range? Was it 1992 through what year?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Well, formally until December 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So I'd like to concentrate your testimony on the time period that you were first deputy, then secretary general of the Presidency. Could you tell the Court briefly what your duties were in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Well, apart from being deputy secretary general and secretary general, I continued to act as adviser for general legal affairs and secretary of the Commission for Pardons. This was the period when some advisers, who were ethnic Serbs, had left Sarajevo. So these posts remained vacant and therefore I had to do that work as well. Basically, as deputy secretary general and as secretary general, I was Chief of Administration. So questions that were resolved in that domain primarily had to do with preparing sessions of the Presidency, preparing the material that would be discussed at Presidency sessions, work on having proper copies provided for all the members of the Presidency, scheduling Presidency sessions, setting the agenda, and so on and so forth, and of course attending sessions of the Presidency itself, where I had the right to participate in the debate, but I did not have the right to vote.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, before we get into the actual Presidency sessions, could you please tell the Chamber what constituted the Presidency in 1992 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Well, the Presidency had two representatives respectively of the constituent peoples, two Croats, two Serbs, two Muslims. I'm going to say "Muslims," although they're called "Bosniaks" nowadays, and I find it easier to still call them "Muslims," and it really corresponds to the truth, because that's what we called them in those days. So two Croats, two Serbs, two Muslims respectively, and one from the others -- other ethnic groups. It was Ganic, specifically, in this case. He was a candidate of the Yugoslavs, and that is how he won the election. According to the provisions of the then Constitution, in conditions of war that started in 1992, the Presidency was an expanded Presidency consisting of three additional representatives, too; namely, the Prime Minister, the President of the Assembly, and the commander-in-chief of the army, no matter what this person's rank was. According to the Constitution, this person was called this or that, but, anyway, it was the person who commanded the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. So if my math is correct, during times where -- normal times, there were seven members of the Presidency; is that what you -- and then during these --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Then ten in conditions of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Are these numbers required by any law?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was set in the Constitution and the Rules of Procedure of the Presidency, but I'm not sure. I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know what role the Presidency played in times of war?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Well, in times of war the Presidency, in addition to its other functions, took over the function of the Assembly, the Parliament, that is, but also I think that this is what the Trial Chamber will be more interested in, the Presidency was practically the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: At this time I would like the witness to be shown P000042. It's an exhibit -- oh, excuse me, Exhibit number 42 from the law library. And particularly -- this is a long document, but if we could scroll to -- it's Article 222, which in the B/C/S version is page 22, I believe, in English it's 108 and 109. If we could zoom in on Article 222.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you identify what this document is, or this part of the document?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Precisely what I've been talking about now. I don't know what this is. It may be the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, sorry to make you do this, Mr. Usher. Can we see the first page of the document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I still can't see what this is about. Sorry, this is just the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If you could read -- scroll down and see if you come to any point where you can --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the Constitution, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now can we go back to Article 222. So this is the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was in effect in 1992 to 1994. Okay. Now, Article 22 --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry. Article 222 discusses, in the second paragraph -- well, excuse me, the first paragraph: "During the period of martial law, the composition of the Presidency is extended to improve the President of the assembly, the President of the government, and the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff in the armed forces of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Is that what that says?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Then the Constitution goes on to say that "During the period of martial law, the Presidency is the Supreme Command of armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And one more sentence: "The extended Presidency during the period of martial law organises and directs the defence of all forms of national resistance on the territory of the Republic." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We may put away this exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there were sessions. Can you tell us what these sessions were? In other words, were they regularly-scheduled sessions or did an event have to happen in order for sessions to arise?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the situation. Generally, we had sessions at least once a month. However, depending on what was going on or what kind of degrees with the force of law were supposed to be adopted, and depending on the political situation, sometimes they would be scheduled three to four times a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And were you present -- can you -- were you present at most of these meetings during your tenure as deputy and secretary general?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us, during the time that you held these posts, approximately how many sessions there might have been, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I really cannot recall. Tons of them, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, were these sessions tape-recorded?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. Again, it depended on the facilities we had. May I remind you that at that time in Sarajevo there was no electricity, no water, no heating, things like that. However, for the needs of the Presidency, we had two generators, or was it one - I cannot remember exactly - that we used precisely for that, in order to have the Presidency sessions recorded. I cannot say for sure whether they were all recorded, but at the end of all the minutes, it would say whether the session had been tape-recorded. If so, it says that that recording constitutes an integral part of the material from that session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If -- were there other means of recording what occurred during the sessions if, for instance, there was no electricity?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It would happen that minutes would be done in hand. They would be handwritten. This was usually done by my deputy, Alija Selimovic, who regrettably died in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, could you just explain briefly to the Chamber the logistics in terms of the tape-recording? You -- presume you had some subordinates, and what would they do prior to the meetings and during the meetings and then after the meetings, what would they do with the tape-recordings or minutes of the sessions?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: As for the tape-recording of the sessions, there were two men who were in charge of that. One was Ibro Delic, and the other one who was a professional and who had been doing this in the assembly and then was transferred to us, it was a man called Kemal, Kemo. Unfortunately, I don't know his last name, but for many years he worked on that in the Assembly, and he often helped out in the Presidency. They would prepare the room for the recordings. There was another group of people who worked on the reproduction of documents, if there was enough time for that, and then this would be distributed to members of the Presidency, along with an invitation to attend the session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And approximately how long would these meetings last?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Again, it depended on the items on the agenda. I can tell you one thing, that not a single session was short and none of them were less than two hours long.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And after the sessions were over, were the tape-recordings taken to a particular place and then transcribed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, because we had a typing pool. Typists worked in this pool. They were top professionals. They did excellent work, and they worked in the Presidency practically from its very inception. To use their professional jargon, they transcribed the sessions, everything that had been said or, rather, everything that had been recorded on these audiotapes, they directly typed out as a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then were the transcripts and tape-recordings stored in someplace, archives or somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were stored -- or rather the originals were stored in the archives. Later on, I found out -- well, to tell you the truth, this is something that I did not have to worry about at the time. The tapes were stored in a special safe, and the transcripts in archives. However, copies of all of these transcripts and minutes, if any of the members of the Presidency expressed an interest in seeing what was in the entire transcript, then these copies would be submitted to members of the Presidency and every one of the members of the Presidency had the right to ask for the transcript of a session where he had participated in the discussion, particularly that section that pertained to his own remarks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, just to back up a minute, when after the transcripts were prepared, were they reviewed by anyone or by everyone in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No. All members of the Presidency would have the entire minutes by the next session. The minutes were actually an abbreviated version of the transcripts. And at every following session, they would agree to what had been said at the previous session. That was always the first item on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What types of matters were discussed at these Presidency sessions?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, these were questions that pertained, for instance, to supplies, power sources, the adoption of legal documents, decrees during the war, then appointments that the Presidency was in charge of, starting with diplomatic representatives to the directors of some public companies and things like that. Of course, the situation in Sarajevo itself was discussed, too, precisely because of what I was saying a few moments ago, that even the most basic supplies were not available at times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were military matters discussed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No, no, never, in the sense of discussing some kind of military strategy or operations or individual actions, no. These were not subjects that the Presidency dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did the subject of the Mujahedin ever come up at any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not, never. I heard about the Mujahedin in 1999. This really was never a topic of discussion at Presidency meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, apart from -- now, you just said "meetings." Do you mean meetings or sessions?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Sessions, sessions. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, were most of these sessions public?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, were there instances where the sessions would not be public and would not be recorded?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but usually the president would first make such a proposal to the members of the Presidency, and then a decision would be taken by all members to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you tell us what some of the matters might have been or were that were not subject to recordings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Usually, as far as I can remember, I cannot say with certainty, but usually if it was assumed that certain individuals who may have been proposed for certain positions in Bosnia or outside of Bosnia would be discussed, and that there might be divergent views about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, do you recall a session where General Delic was discussed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: The first time that I personally heard of Mr. Delic was, I think, at the beginning of the summer of 1993, when General Halilovic was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you recall the session at which this occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well, because Halilovic's replacement was a major surprise for me. I think even he was surprised. I hadn't heard anything about it before that, nor was I aware of it, so that I was extremely surprised when President Izetbegovic made this proposal to dismiss Halilovic and appoint Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you recall what time of day the appointment was made?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I can tell you approximately, and based on my own experience regarding session times, it could have been between 10.00 and 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But as you sit here today, you don't recall the date, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No, no. I remember that it was early in the summer, but exactly what date it was, I really can't remember. Shall we say June, the beginning of June, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, apart from the formal Presidency sessions, whether they were public or private and recorded, were there other meetings that you were aware of that took place of members of the Presidency -- which included members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were, and it wasn't just that I was aware of them; everyone knew about them. These were meetings attended by certain members of the Presidency, the president, and usually the man in charge of the army. Earlier, it was Halilovic, and later, Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And who were the other members that generally attended these other meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Well, Ganic, Haris Silajdzic, as far as I can remember, yes, he too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Was either Ganic or Mr. Silajdzic the president of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No, but Silajdzic was the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Correct. But pursuant to Article 222, the Presidency was extended to include the president of the Assembly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What position did Mr. Ganic hold?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: He, too, was a member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were any other members of the Presidency in attendance at these private meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Was a person by the name of Miro Lazovic present?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: It says "Miro Lasic," but I can't say straightaway that neither Miro Lasic or Miro Lazovic ever attended, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
