utterances.text: Yes, I was going to question you about both of them, but I did say "Lazovic." Do you recall what position Mr. Lazovic held at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Miro Lazovic was the president of the Assembly, and Miro Lazovic was a member of the Presidency on behalf of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know who Franjo Boras was?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He, too, was a member of the Presidency on behalf of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And was he in attendance at these private meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know, particularly as Franjo Boras did not spend most of the time of the war in Sarajevo, he was not in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know who Mirko Pejanovic was or is?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Mirko Pejanovic was a member of the Presidency. And if you're asking me what he is now, he's a professor at the university.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did he attend these private meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us the ethnic composition of the four persons that you mentioned who were in the attendance at these private meetings, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, were other members of the Presidency -- let me rephrase that, please. Were you aware whether any other members of the Presidency were upset at these meetings, the fact that these meetings occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that they were disturbed or upset. They were -- it would be better to say that they were curious about what was going on there, and they talked about it amongst themselves. I'm referring to the people who were outside that group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's correct, thank you. Now, do you know what was discussed at these private meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I really have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of an operation called Operation Trebevic --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Excuse my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I know which specific Trebevic operation you are referring to. There were attempts to make a breakthrough at Trebevic, which is a mountain in the vicinity of Sarajevo. If, if you're referring to one of those operations, or perhaps an operation which settled accounts with the criminal groups in Sarajevo, if that is how it was called.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the operation that settled accounts with criminal groups in Sarajevo. You're familiar with that; okay. Now, was the topic of criminal groups discussed at all in the sessions or mentioned in the sessions?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: At Presidency sessions, there was frequent mention of criminal groups who were out of control of the police and the army and which are not within the system of subordination. They were mistreating citizens, looting them, and that something had to be done about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Was there any further discussion other than something had to be done about them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No. I assume that the plan of the operation itself, the way it was implemented and the rest, was agreed upon at one of those closed meetings which was not attended by the other members of the Presidency, because I knew nothing about it, and I would have known had it been discussed at Presidency sessions. I mean, I didn't know anything about the details of the operation, nor when it would take place, nor how it would take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, on Wednesday evening, two evenings ago, and yesterday afternoon, did you have an opportunity to review transcripts and/or minutes of Presidency sessions that occurred during 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you recall today approximately -- I mean, do you recall right now how many sessions you reviewed, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. I didn't look at them all in detail, but I did most of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we have a moment, please? Thank you. You. Okay. Thank you, Your Honours. Sorry. Your Honours, at this time -- well, one further question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you determine that you were present at most of the meetings that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Again, we are talking about sessions. Here it says "meetings."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Thank you for correcting me. The session -- the minutes and transcripts that you reviewed, were you --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And when we attended the proofing session, were there some meetings that you realised you had not attended?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you recall the number of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but maybe 15 or so, 12 to 15. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you reviewed the transcripts of the sessions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: From your review of these documents, does that -- does it support your testimony -- well, you said to your memory the Mujahedin was never discussed at these sessions?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were never discussed, as far as I can remember, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point we would like to admit in evidence the transcripts and minutes of the sessions. We have -- although they were premarked at individual sessions, we have put them into e-court under one exhibit number -- or two exhibits numbers, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor has informed us about this in a letter. We discussed it, and I do not object for the Prosecutor to tender this document in this way. But during the cross-examination of the witness, I will certainly be using the exhibits that were in the e-court earlier because it would be most confusing me to use parts of this exhibit that is being tendered by the Prosecutor. I think the five TOs that had been entered into the e-court can be used by us without any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio, you are not planning to tender a whole lengthy documents on minutes of the sessions; you're going to tender parts that you are dealing with?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour. We are tendering the minutes of all the sessions. There are approximately 58 sessions, and they total about 900 and some odd pages. And the reason is to show that this issue was never discussed. So unless you have the full document, I don't see how they can be of the value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want us now to read through 900 pages to determine that the issue was not talked about?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have the witness's testimony and the documents, and you may look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the witness has testified that the issue was never discussed, unless it is controverted by some other evidence, why shouldn't we believe it? Why should we have 900 pages to support that point?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I would encourage you to believe the witness, but the documents are to substantiate the witness's testimony. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But they can only substantiate the witness's testimony if we are going to read through 900 pages to determine one little point, that this issue was never discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, it may -- it may become contentious later on, Your Honour. The decision was made and the trial strategy of the case to introduce the transcript of these meetings through Mr. Djuricic, and that's what we're here to do today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that may have been the strategy. You're saying what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I mean, there may be other witnesses who may speak about other parts of these transcripts -- of these sessions. I'm not -- I can't say that right now. I don't know if that's -- that is in the future, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think there's any problem, other people talking about parts of the transcript. What is the point, if I understand you clearly, you want to tender into evidence 900 pages of documentation to support one little fact, that -- the question of what? The Mujahedin, was never discussed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, that the Mujahedin was never discussed and it was a very important topic for the Presidency that was the supreme command of the army, and the Prosecution would suggest that it is compelling evidence and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Carry on, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. And the Prosecution requests that these be admitted as support for its case. We're not asking the Court to read 900 pages of documents this afternoon. It is part of the record for the entire Prosecution case, because -- to substantiate what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that you want us to read them this afternoon, but you want us to read them sometime in the future before judgement is written. I'm just wondering whether this is good use of the resources, to read 900 pages to determine that Mujahedin was not discussed, when the witness has told us it was not discussed. Maybe, if I may just turn to the Defence on this point before we make a ruling on this point. Is this a disputed fact, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour, of course it is disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I would imagine that if it is disputed, at the relevant time the Defence would refer us to the relevant pages of the 900 pages to show where it was discussed. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you want me to respond to Judge Harhoff's -- I wasn't sure I was supposed to hear that. Do you want it to be marked for identification at this point in time, Your Honour? We will be happy to mark it for identification at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not happy to mark it for identification because I'm not quite sure whether marking it for identification means -- absolves me from reading it, and I don't want to read it if only to determine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just intervene. The suggestion was made by me. My idea was that if we mark the 900 pages now for identification, then the Defence will take us to the particular pages in those 900 pages where war matters or Mujahedin are discussed, and then we end up saving those pages into evidence. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the same way as the Prosecutor is saying, in general terms, that the matter was not discussed, the Defence will assert in a similar way that it was discussed, without indicating the specific pages, as the Prosecutor hasn't done. I have tried, in the same way as you, talking to Madam Sartorio. I said that we would like to be clearly informed on which pages of those exhibits the Prosecutor wishes to rely on to be able to prepare our defence, and I tried to indicate to the Prosecution that this was a major problem. But the Prosecutor decided to use it in this way. I don't mind, but you will see, from the cross-examination, which is not the time now for me to discuss in detail, it is not quite as simple as the Prosecutor claims, and I don't think it was a good solution for exhibits to be tendered into evidence in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. The Prosecution originally was going to introduce each session individually, but that, in our assessment, was going to be a huge, incredible waste of time to introduce the minutes of 54 sessions, which is why we did it in bulk. And the reason we're introducing them is to prove a negative, so there aren't specific pages that are more important than other pages. The Prosecution's position is that the entire lot of documents, all of the minutes of the sessions, are relevant to the proof that it's held to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll mark the 900 pages for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll identify the exhibit number for identification. It's P06193A and P0 -- excuse me. P06193, then P06193A, and we have provided an index of these documents, and that can be found at P06193B. Just another question, Your Honour. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, not yet. We've got to give an exhibit number to what you have just been telling us, and I'm not sure whether you want three exhibit numbers or you want one exhibit number. I don't know how these things go.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We had to split up the documents into two exhibit numbers rather than the one we wanted to use because of the length of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then you have given us three -- three of numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The third number -- 6193 is the first lot of sessions; 6193A, the second lot; and then for purposes of reference we've provided an index of the documents, and we have had to enter that into e-court separately as 6193B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've told us that. Now, those are three separate documents. Do you want three --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we ask that these three documents be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but under three exhibit numbers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's three parts of one exhibit number. It's the same exhibit number, 6193, but it's plain 6193, then 6193A and B, so it's three parts to one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told that you will have to use three exhibit numbers for these.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number P06193B, which is the list or the index, will be Exhibit number 307; 65 ter number P06193 will be MFI 308; and 65 ter number P06193A, the supplemental document, will be MFI 308.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Wait a minute, it looks like you've given us -- now, you have given us two numbers only, sir. I would expected you to go up to 309.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might repeat those numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first 65 ter number is P06193B, which is the index.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That was being assigned MFI 307.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: MFI 307, right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number P06193 will be MFI 308.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the supplemental list of documents, which is 65 ter number P06193A, will be MFI 309.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's better. Thank you so much. And on that note, I think we can take a break, unless this is not a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I just have one more question on direct, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I would just like to, sir, bring you back to the session at which General Delic was appointed commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and ask you if you know the point in time when the appointment was effective. Was it effective at that point?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was a decision that was effective immediately. From the afternoon of that day, Mr. Delic was the commander-in-chief of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take an adjournment and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic. Cross-examination by Madam Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djuricic. I will be putting questions to you today on behalf of the Defence of General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: First of all, you're a Bosnian Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, since the war. Until then, I was a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you spent part of your career as a judge of the Second Municipal Court. Then you worked in the Ministry of Justice, and when working there, you were responsible for supervising the work of court throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That involved supervision over the work of offices of prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Well, to a lesser degree. I mainly focused on courts of law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Whatever, you do know how offices of the prosecutors worked?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You explained to us that in 1992, you worked as a legal adviser to the entire Presidency, and then a secretary general. In actual fact, did I understand this correctly, you were chief of administration of the Presidency, including certain financial aspects?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you something about sessions of the Presidency, in general terms. Sessions of the Presidency were recorded, or at least minutes were kept; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, in relation to these handwritten minutes, you told us that sessions lasted very long, at least two hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: That's right. I don't even remember any exceptions of less than two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You also told us that you looked through all these minutes. The Prosecutor showed you these minutes; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that sessions that had handwritten minutes were very short? These minutes are two or three handwritten pages; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: That's right, and the handwriting is not all that legible, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree that these two or three handwritten pages do not reflect at all what happened at these sessions; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now I'm going to go back to the members of the Presidency, and then yet again to these sessions. Please, all members of the Presidency, regardless of their ethnic affiliation, took part in the sessions on an equal footing; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, these sessions of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now we are talking about sessions of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, on a fully equal footing, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And they made decisions on an equal footing; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you agree that all members of the Presidency from time to time visited parts of the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including civilian institutions, but also barracks and defence lines? You know that because you authorised their travel, you issued these travel authorisations, am I right, for their per diems, and whatever?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure about these per diems as for touring the defence lines around Sarajevo, no per diems were issued for that. But I can say with certainty that Pejanovic and Tatjana Mijatovic did go to the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In other words, they toured military barracks, defence lines, corps? That was the essence of my question.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about outside Sarajevo, but I know that they did go to the lines in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo, and they visited headquarter staffs that were in Sarajevo itself, at least the two persons I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness please take a look at D296 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at page 1. The date is, say, the 16th of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Tour of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it says: "A member of the Presidency of RBH, Mrs. Tatjana Ljujic-Mijatovic, will make a tour of the free territory --" And Zenica, Travnik, Vares, Breza, Orlavo [phoen] are referred to. So do you agree, first of all, that Mrs. Ljujic-Mijatovic was a Serb member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you agree that she went outside the territory of Sarajevo and toured these municipalities, that this is what the document says?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I don't know whose document this is. Is it a document of the Presidency or of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I mean, I can talk about documents that I, myself, signed perhaps or knew of. It fits into what you said just now because Tatjana did go out and visit the lines of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness please look at paragraph 8 on the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just briefly, could you take a look? Do you agree the signature is General Delic's here, and do you agree with me that paragraph 8 says: "The Corps Commands, as the delegation visits the areas of responsibility, should provide transport and security for the delegation where the delegation is touring, the zone of responsibility, and paragraph 9 says: A plan should be drawn up for the tour and presented to Mrs. Tatjana Ljujic. In other words, she is allowed to take part in drafting the plan of the visit?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That stems from the document that we see.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could this document please be assigned an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, let me just establish one point with you, Witness. Does this document arise out of the Presidency of which you were secretary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is a document of the Supreme Command Staff of Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not with my line of work or the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document -- yes, Madam. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number 310.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, please, in response to the question put by the Presiding Judge, you said that this document has nothing to do with the work of the Presidency. Do you agree, actually, that this refers to a visit by the Presidency and its Serb member, Tatjana Ljujic-Mijakovic, a member of the Presidency, who is touring the field?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No doubt that Tatjana was a member of the Presidency and that here she is touring the troops of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a member of the Presidency. However, this order has nothing to do with the Presidency. It's not a decision that was signed by -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, yes, thank you, that was the point of my question. Please, now I'm going to go back to the sessions. The sessions were prepared in advance; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Exceptionally, if an urgent matter cropped up, then the president would call me, and I would telephone the other members of the Presidency to tell them that there was an urgent matter that had to be reviewed at a session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. In principle, in advance you would receive draft decisions that had already been written out?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: These drafts were made by various sponsors, government agencies, government bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: And Commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Proposals had no legal force before being adopted; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Precisely. This was a worthless piece of paper if a decision of the Presidency had not been made in this regard and not signed by the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honour, I would like the witness to have a look at document MFI 160.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: This is a document entitled "Proposal for the Presidency," dated the 2nd of June, 1993, and could you please take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: You're putting a question to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Obviously, this document is just a proposal for organisational and personnel changes in the armed forces. This paper is valueless while it was still submitted to us as a proposal. This is a legal technical thing that you are certainly aware of. It existed before the war, too, and now. The sponsor of a proposal makes a draft, lists, say, persons who are supposed to be leaders in the military. Their names are given in a certain order. But only once the Presidency makes a decision adopting this kind of proposal and once the president of the Presidency signs this kind of document, then it would have the legal force of a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you for such an exhaustive explanation, Witness. Could you please just look at the last page of this document. Can we see where the signature is, please? So do you agree that this is not the final document, what we see here?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No, this is not a decision. There is no signature, it doesn't say at what session it was adopted. It doesn't say who attended the session and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, could the document please be put aside, or rather, Your Honours, I would like it to be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even though it's not signed?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, because in the Pre-Trial Brief the Prosecutor used it and referred to it as a final document, as if it were a document that had been adopted, but now we've received an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the document please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, then it will be marked Exhibit 160.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be put aside now, and I'm going to ask you now about the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Madam Vidovic. I have a difficulty in admitting this last document into evidence because I thought that the principle that we have established for admission of documents into evidence was that -- through a witness, was that there would have to be a relation shown between the document and the witness. Otherwise, that document would be inadmissible through that witness. And I was just wondering if there is any link between the witness and this document. He seems to not know of it, and it's only a draft. Its value is questionable. So could you please clarify the link between the document and the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, you have heard His Honour. I asked you questions in connection with the proposal coming up for discussion at the Presidency meeting, and Their Honours are asking what your connection is to this document. Isn't it true that you prepared documents for sessions of the Presidency; they prepared them, not literally?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: The documents such as this one was just one of thousands that reached the Presidency and that were distributed or should be distributed to all Presidency members for them to be able to comment on such a proposal. Now, what you asked me was whether this was a proposal or a decision. My answer is that it was a proposal. It is of no value unless it has been discussed and signed by the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In other words, this was a proposal for a session to be held on the 8th of June, 1993, so this is something directly linked to your work; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I cannot say which particular session was involved, nor do I remember this particular paper. And if it was a proposal, I am sure that I must have received it and distributed it to the other Presidency members.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is that sufficient now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It isn't sufficient, but I'll have to take a reservation on it. So I will dissent [Realtime transcript read in error "assent"] From the opinion to admit it. Thanks. Excuse me. For the record, I said I will dissent.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's no problem. I can withdraw the proposal to tender this document, if you feel that that would be more appropriate. I just wanted to hear the explanation of the witness. Thank you. And may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I do not wish to change your views, so let us just proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The Prosecution has shown you a series of minutes from sessions, and recordings of meetings that you attended, or General Delic, or General Siber or Divjak; isn't that so? Now, in that connection, I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, could the witness see D311, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: This is a list of documents and sessions shown to you by the Prosecution. And in preparations for this trial, the date is the 16th of August of this year. And will you please pay attention --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I spoke to the witness earlier on. I know that he speaks and reads English, so we're actually just referring to the numbers of these sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So in this central column, will you look at the numerical indication for the sessions?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: You mean, the 4th, the 15th, the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. These were mostly sessions for which the attendees are indicated, and these were sessions that you, yourself, attended, and you said yourself that you did not attend some of them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: However, at some sessions your presence cannot be established at all. For example, the 205th session, dated the 5th of July, 1993. I will refer to Exhibit 1384, P01384, then 229th session of the 26th of November, P1630 and P1631, then the 234th session, held on the 2nd of January, 1994, P1670. We have these minutes, but it is not possible to establish the presence of this witness at those sessions. Let me ask you something else in connection with this list. The Prosecution showed you minutes from the 8th of June, 1993, until the 22nd of June, 1994. Would you agree with me that by the ordinal numbers of the sessions, one can see that some are missing? Look on page 1. You will see "204th, 205th, 206th," and then "208th, 211th, 212th," 211th is missing, and then you have the 213th missing. And then if we can look at the next page of this document. By reviewing these documents, if you look at this page, you will see the 218th, 219th, 220th, 225th, are missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please ask the witness questions. You know, you're telling us what we can see, and I think we're taking a lot of time you testifying instead of you asking the witness questions. Why don't you establish all these things you are saying by asking questions to the witness rather than making such a long speech? I'm not sure where you're going with this speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have no translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I thought it would take less time if I did it this way, Your Honour, but I will ask the witness the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't know what you're saying. You're just telling us things that we can see, and we don't know what is the point you want to establish. Ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you agree that sessions were recorded in chronological order?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I assume so, but I have to draw your attention to the fact that minutes, the missing minutes, were the subject of a special investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is the following: You, yourself, did not review them before this trial, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you don't know what was discussed at those sessions?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Of course not. Even when I reviewed the minutes of sessions that I did attend, it took time for me to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You also don't know who attended those sessions?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Would you agree that it is absolutely not necessary for someone to attend from the Supreme Command Staff for the question of the Mujahedin to be discussed; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Izetbegovic himself could have spoken about it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The Minister of Internal affairs, Bakir Alispahic, could have talked about it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Bakir was not present at sessions frequently, but he would come with respect to particular issues and at the invitation of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Would you agree that the question of the Mujahedin was a security question, in a sense?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: In a sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: According to regulations, wouldn't that be within the purview of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, when we are talking about entry into the country, documents and things like that, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. So you can talk to us here only about the sessions which you attended?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, also if you remind me, because it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would now like to focus on the recorded sessions that you have already discussed. If this document can be put away, and could the witness now see P1752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want us to do with this? Do you want us to admit it or do you not want to admit it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Yes, could it be, please, admitted into evidence and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 311.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Counsel, microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1752 now. For the record, until we see the document, it is minutes of the 249th session of the Presidency, held on the 15th of June, 1994, which I am using as an example.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, will you please look at page 1. And then could the witness immediately see page 6 of the Bosnian and English versions, page 6 of the Bosnian and English versions, please. Witness, will you please pay attention to the end of this document. Do you agree -- could Their Honours also see the English version, please. Could you roll it up a little so that we can see the bottom. Thank you. Witness, will you please look at the words where it says "tape-recording," "magnetic tape-recording," and would you agree that the minutes are recorded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 4, Your Honour, the last two sentences.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was customary for the minutes to end with these words.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And would you agree that the transcript of a recorded session is complete if it is -- if it ends in this way?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the transcript or the minutes? The minutes are complete, and then as I explained earlier on, the tape-recordings were taken down and transcribed in the typing bureau, and then it was complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: When we're talking about the minutes, then it must end in this way?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it must if it is a tape-recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this document be given an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Otherwise, if the minutes do not end in this manner, it means that it is not complete?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No, it means that no tape-recording was made unless this sentence appears, where it says that "the magnetic tape-recording shall constitute a component part of the minutes." It would mean that the session was not tape-recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That is helpful, too. Could this document be given an exhibit number, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll ask the question I asked earlier. Notwithstanding that this has not been signed by anybody?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I can see, these minutes were always like this. They were never signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't hear the witness say "yes." The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 312.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this document be put away and could the witness see P1579. Until we see the document on the screen, for the record, it is the minutes of the 221st session of the Presidency, held on the 18th of October, 1993. And I have chosen a handwritten report from that session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 5 of this document. Page 5, please. Can we see the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the end of the document [indiscernible]? You're talking about the English --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, would you agree that sessions of which the minutes were written by hand, it should have an end indicating who chaired the meeting, who took down the minutes and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: That would usually be stated at the top of the document, that is, those present, and that applies to all minutes, including those written by hand. I don't know the reasons for the minutes being taken in this way. Probably there was no electricity. But in practice, we accepted such minutes as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But do you agree that we can't see whether this is the end or whether the session ended?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: If that is the end of the document, then it hasn't been completed in a regular manner, because the words -- it should state the session ended at such-and-such an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we scroll down to the end of the English version, please. Can we scroll down to the end of the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now see document 313. It is the transcribed recording of a meeting in 1993. Will you please look at page 2 of this document, which is page 2 of the English version, too, dated on the 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it a "P" document or "D" document? Is it "D313" or is it "P313"?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D313, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it also has a "P" number. But to avoid confusion, we decided to do it in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, will you please look. We've seen page 1. Could the witness first be shown the first page of the document to see for himself that it is the transcribed recording of a session held on the 18th of October, 1993. We have it now in English, but the Bosnian version, too, please. Thank you very much. Now, please look at page 2 of this document. You can see Tape 8 through 6. Now please look at page 3 of the document. And in Bosnian too. Do you agree that we see here that the rest of the session is inaudible?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So we've seen that on the previous tape, only a few sentences have been described, whereas here we see that the rest of the session is inaudible, so you cannot know what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Of course not. There must have been a fault in the electricity supply. The lines went down, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Very well. And the sessions continued, however, even if there was no electricity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We are a bit puzzled, Counsel, about the probative value of these documents. What is it, exactly, that you are trying to show? I thought, from the discussion that we had before the break, that your point was to say that, yes, military matters were indeed discussed during the Presidency meetings, but I'm not sure this document provides much support to that assertion. But could you explain what it is you want the Bench to extract from this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I would like the Bench to conclude is that we do not have the complete set of minutes from sessions and that we don't know what was discussed at the other remaining sessions. To be more specific, whether the question of Mujahedin was discussed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want to ask a question. Can I ask a question, again for my own understanding of the proceedings, I would like to follow what is happening in court. If it is established finally that Mujahedin was discussed or not discussed, where does it take us in the case? What is the point of discussing Mujahedin in the Presidency? What is it intended to show in this case? I didn't understand it when the Prosecution did it, I still don't understand it. I would like to be enlightened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'm not sure it's appropriate to talk about the particular evidence and what its relevance is to the entire case in trial and also in front of a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why is that not appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, because we're going to be discussing here what parts -- what a part of the evidence, a part of the puzzle, suggests in the overall picture of the case, in front of the witness, and at the beginning of the case in front of Defence counsel. I'm not sure either side is really prepared or wants to do that at this point in time for particular pieces of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've often heard this kind of excuse in this Tribunal, and I've never understood what it means. You're coming again with something that -- I don't understand why it cannot be explained in the presence of a witness, the purpose of their evidence. If the purpose of their evidence is to show either that -- I can't even begin to use this example because I don't understand this point, but I've never really understood why a reason for evidence cannot be given if the witness is in court. On the other hand, if you are not able to discuss this, then you're running the risk of losing the Bench. I don't understand what we are -- I have not understood the purpose for calling this witness so far, and if you lose me, you've lost me. So, I mean, I may or may never see the relevance of this evidence unless it is explained to me at some stage, and I'm speaking here for myself. I'm not speaking for the entire Chamber. I'm just saying I don't understand what we are doing this afternoon. And you may decide not to explain the relevance of this. Do understand that if you do that, you're running the risk of losing the Bench or at least some of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll explain briefly, Your Honour. But the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not going to force you to explain. If you don't want to explain things in front of the witness, I'm not forcing you to. I'm just saying: Know the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I have a gun to my head. Well, Your Honour, in brief, the Prosecution's position is that in times of martial law, according to the Constitution and according to what was in practice, there was a presidency. The Presidency consisted of ten members. It was multicultural members, and the Presidency was in charge, and the supreme commander of the Armed Forces, which means the Presidency should have made decisions on command-and-control issues and other items that should have been discussed regarding the operation of the army during this time period. These matters were not discussed at the Presidency meetings, pursuant to the Constitution. Rather, they were discussed in private meetings, of which this witness and no one was allowed to be present, and decisions were made. But decisions were made, as the witness discussed. There were general discussions about criminal groups in the Presidency sessions, but nothing was ever resolved. But then somehow things got resolved. So they got resolved as a result of other private meetings, not the Presidency sessions at which the Constitution required that these issues be resolved. That's the purpose of this evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Actually, you've just given us a summary of the evidence. Thank you so much for the summary of the evidence, and I hear what you say is the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To the extent that you refer to the constitutional obligations, and I think that could have been given in a very short, cryptic sentence just to say, "We want to check whether the constitutional obligations were carried out by the Presidency." But be that as it may, I hear what you say. Madam, I don't know whether Judge -- okay. May this document then be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 314.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 314. Madam Vidovic, excluding the time that I took talking, you've actually gone through your 39 minutes that was taken by the Prosecution in lead, but Judge Lattanzi has something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I had one thing. I was waiting for the translation into French. The translation into French is sometimes a bit lengthy, and is finished after the English translation. But I'm not really sure that it is -- the fact about the parties telling about their case in front of the witness, I do reserve my position when it comes to this, the parties giving their case in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand that I have used up my time, but in view of your explanation of the position of the Prosecution, you will understand that I have a few more important questions for this witness. We had expected the examination to take a little longer, and some things are very important for us that the witness has discussed. So would you please indulge me for a few more minutes? Thank you. If the witness could now be shown the session held on the 8th of June, P1194. For the record, it is the 203rd session held on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It is the session, Witness, which I don't know whether you saw these minutes. By contents, it would appear that it was at this session that Rasim Delic was appointed. Will you please first focus your attention on page 5 of this document. 5, please. Will you please look at the 3rd paragraph. Pejanovic is speaking. Can the English version be rolled down, please. Will you look at what Pejanovic says. He says that: This is a complex question. He requests information about Trebevic, how many were killed, who ordered the action. He was consulted about those proposals. He does not think that the Staff should be consulted, but suggests consulting Siber and Divjak. Then look further down, line 6. It says he proposes that the question of ranks be postponed, and the one-but-last line of the Bosnian version, which is on the next page of the English version - could we see the next page of the English version, please - he proposes that the Presidency should take decisions on all personnel issues - that is at the top of the page - that the Presidency should decide on all personal issues in the corps. Would you agree, when testifying a moment ago, you said that military issues were not reviewed at sessions? Let us first clear up what you imply when you say "military issues." Did I understand you correctly, you meant "military operations"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, military operations, strategy, the units that would be involved, and it was logical, in my view, that such things should not be discussed at the Presidency for the simple reason that there were many people present, and there would be many divergent views. Everyone would have his view, and many of them were not qualified for military issues. And something else. In Bosnia we had three nations fighting one another. Muslims, as a nation. There was harmonisation on a national basis as applied to the other two nations. And it was logical for me that in a war that they were waging a war against both the other two nations, it would be normal for me that such matters be discussed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But do you agree that strategic issues were issued such appointments?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: All the appointments in the army, and even in the police were made at the Presidency, where the actual decision was made, but decisions regarding corps commands, the appointments of high ranks, even in the police and in the military and civilian police, all these appointments were discussed at Presidency meetings. I said that earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now will you please look at the last line of page 6 in the Bosnian version, which is again page 6 of the English version. You see it says the continuation will be at 1400 hours. Could we roll down the text, please? That's right. "Resumption at 1400 hours." Your Honour, I need to see page 6 of the Bosnian version as well. I'm not sure that that is the right page of the Bosnian version. It's the next page. Here we are, yes. You see it says: "Resumption at 1400 hours." Now, will you move the page down for you to see it in the Bosnian version. Now let us see the next page of the Bosnian version. Testifying this morning, you said that you believed that General Delic was appointed about 10.00 or 11.00 -- at about 10.00 or 11.00?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I can tell you the proposal that Mr. Delic be appointed instead of Sefer Halilovic was made at the first part of this session between 10.00 and 11.00, and then there was a break because somebody - I don't remember who - wanted to consult his deputies, Divjak and Siber, whether they agreed with such a replacement, because Sefer Halilovic said that his deputies supported him and that his dismissal could cause unrest in the army. I remember that session specifically because I was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please now look at the very end of the document, that a commission was set up for the handing over of duty between Sefer Halilovic and -- the next page, please, the previous page, the previous pages that we had on the screen, please. That's right. Now can we have the appropriate page in English? We had it there a moment ago. Will you look, please? Do you agree, and it says, point 2: "The situation in Gorazde ..." And then it says: "Sefer Halilovic," and then it says: "The handing over of duty between Sefer and Rasim Delic" -- I'm sorry, below that: "The situation in Gorazde...," read the report of the units in Srebrenica, 1st Corps, that Pejanovic should go, Sefer --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I can't see it, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 7 in English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Sefer handed in his oral resignation, yes, the commission for the handing over, Fikret Muslimovic, Jovan Divjak and Mirsad, I think, Causevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And so do you agree that it was after the break, which took place at 2.00 p.m., that only then was the commission formed for the hand-over of duty?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I thought that the decision came into effect the same day it was made, but obviously it had to come into effect once the hand-over of duty was completed, because this was an urgent thing. The commander-in-chief is important, so this must have -- he must have been promoted to the position of commander in the second part of the session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says here that Jovan Divjak was a member of that commission?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 315.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you a few things about those meetings that the Prosecutor called "private meetings." Do you agree that you did not attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You don't know at all what was discussed there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I absolutely do not know. Perhaps they just drank coffee. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, please, the Prosecutor gave you a series of names of members of the Presidency, including Tatjana Ljujic, mostly non-Muslim names. Do you agree that the Prosecutor did not ask you about Nijaz Durakovic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Who also did not attend, that's true too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you agree that he is a Muslim, and you see he wasn't there with them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Muslim, but he was political opposition, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I accept that, but he's a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: No doubt, he's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And now just one more thing. You saw General Delic many times at these sessions, isn't that right, and generally speaking in the Presidency? Do you agree that he also held meetings with Pejanovic, Komsic, Kljuc, that he did not isolate himself from the other members of the Presidency, that he didn't isolate himself from them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I can also give my personal impression about Mr. Delic from that period of time. I did not have any private contacts with him except during breaks of the sessions. My impression about him was that this was a courteous, decent man who was not a fanatic in any sense, and who was a professional soldier, as I knew JNA officers to be like before. He contacted everyone, and I think that he did different things for members of the Presidency who were non-Muslims, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In other words, he had meetings with Komsic, Pejanovic, and all these other people, too?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Well, he would see them, that's for sure. What they discussed, what the subject of their discussions was, I don't know, but that was my impression of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. You told us just now that your impression of General Delic was that he was a professional. In the previous statement that you gave to the Prosecutor, on several pages you described a terrible situation in Sarajevo, a terrible situation, with the commanders of individual brigades --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection. She's referring to the statement of the witness. It certainly isn't in evidence. The witness is here viva voce. And I think she should either put the questions to the witness, but not refer to a previous statement that he gave and what he may or may not have said in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the first time that I cannot use a statement now that had been given? Of course, I have that statement here, but I am trying -- well, I'm trying to save time. On six pages, at least, the witness described the situation in Sarajevo, and he even described his very own arrest. And even today at one point --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Now she's telling you what's in the statement, she's testifying. I think this is totally inappropriate, what Defence counsel is doing at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic, don't testify. Defend your right to put the question to the witness, if that's what you want to do, without quoting the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, do I understand that the Prosecutor's objection has been sustained, that I cannot rely on the statement that he previously gave to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, you are misunderstanding. I said, "Defend your stand to use the statement to the witness, but do not quote the statement."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, please, is it correct that General Delic, on the 8th of June, when he was appointed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Defend your stand. I have not ruled on the objection, Madam. I must rule on the objection. Defend your stand, in other words, but you don't do that by quoting the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd rather withdraw the question and move on to another question, because I have very little time left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, then the objection becomes sustained.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, please, you were in the Presidency, you were in Sarajevo. It's correct, is it not, that General Delic found a terrible situation there when he came to become commander?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: His appointment coincides with resolving this situation. How big his very own contribution is, I really don't know, but indeed the situation was terrible in Sarajevo. Criminal groups that were armed, they were rendering some kind of justice of their own, looting, mistreating citizens, and so on and so forth. I think that this was sometime in November when the situation was cleared up, and by then Delic had already been well into his commanding post of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we see D210, please. For the transcript, this is an excerpt from the book "Balkan Front: A Military History of the Yugoslav Conflict, 1990-1995," issued by the Central Intelligence Agency of the United States of America in October of 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this document, unless the Defence counsel can lay a foundation of some sort with this witness. I mean, this isn't -- she just mentioned -- I believe that Defence counsel just mentioned something about the Central Intelligence, the CIA. I don't see the relevance of this document, and I wanted to object before she poses a question to the witness and he answers, if he -- I'm not sure what an excerpt from a book, something issued by the CIA of the US, has to do with this particular witness and what he's testified to today about Presidency sessions in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness also testified about the difficult situation in Sarajevo, and precisely in response to my questions he talked about the activities of General Delic that are written about in these parts of the CIA report from October 2003. It has to do with the last part of my questions. I said "D310".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, we have D210.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now it's been changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The script had said "210." Is it 310 you want, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 310. This is the right document, the one that we see on our screens now. And now could we look at page 2 of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute. We've got to rule on the objection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We've got to rule on the objection. You are still in the process of defending why you are bringing this book on the screen. Are you done? Do you want me to make a ruling now?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in addition to what I've said, I have the right to put questions to the witness that is important for my own case during the cross-examination as well. May I add that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The objection is withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness please see page 2 of this document. In the Bosnian, too, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at this document. It says the Bosnian Army is cleaning house, and you talked about Trebevic in relation to Caco and Celo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about the last sentence: "It is very important that the Trebevic action was the first and most dramatic access taken by General Delic towards the professionalisation of the Bosnian Army"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here, and that is the way one can take it as the truth, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you agree that you know and that you were receiving reports in the Presidency that the army had brought criminal charges against many perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember that. I don't know exactly against who, specifically, but I know that some of them were detained, and then they were pardoned, because these were misled soldiers, if I can put it that way, who could have been useful for the defence onwards as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that many of these people were accused of war crimes; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO DJURICIC
utterances.text: I remember that some of them were accused. Who exactly, I don't know, I can't remember any longer, but I can say that after that, after this action, Trebevic-1, life in Sarajevo became normal for the non-Muslim population; that is to say, freedom of movement, there was no more mistreatment, and the things that Caco did arbitrarily, the arbitrary arrests as well, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could this document please be given an exhibit number, and that concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have an exhibit number to this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 316.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Questions from the Bench. Judge? Thank you, sir. This brings us to the conclusion of your testimony, and the Chamber would like to take the opportunity to thank you for taking time off your busy schedule to come and testify. May you travel safely back home. Thank you very much. You are excused and you may now stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
